messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kofi's Vigil

Kofi Mensah has been cutting hair in the same barber shop on Malcolm X Boulevard for twenty-three years. The shop is small, intimate—three stations, a waiting area with magazines from 2019, and a back room where he keeps his supplies. He knows most of his clients by name and by the particular way they like their edges shaped. This work has always grounded him. Until it didn't.

Three months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late September, Kofi was closing up. He had locked the front door and was sweeping near the register when two men pushed through the glass. He remembers the moment with a clarity that feels like watching a film he cannot stop: the sudden crack of his own breath, the larger man's hand on his shoulder, the smell of alcohol—sharp, acrid, unmistakable—flooding his nostrils as the man leaned in close. Kofi remembers the words, the demand, the feeling of his own body becoming separate from his mind, as though he were watching himself hand over the cash drawer from somewhere outside himself. The men left as quickly as they came. Kofi was not physically injured. But something fractured that night.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found himself replaying the robbery like a film stuck on repeat. He would be sweeping the same spot where it happened and suddenly he was there again—seeing the man's face, the thrust of the door, the way the light from the streetlamp caught the edge of the register drawer. These images came without warning and felt utterly real, as though the event were happening in the present moment. What disturbed him most was that he could see everything—every detail burned into his mind like a photograph—yet when he tried to tell his wife Ama what had happened, the words simply would not come. He knew what occurred, knew it in his bones, but the language to describe it seemed to dissolve on his tongue. He would open his mouth and nothing would emerge except a kind of hollow silence.

The smell of alcohol became unbearable. One of his regular clients, a man named Jerome who came in every other Saturday, arrived smelling of beer. Kofi felt his chest tighten, his palms begin to sweat. He made an excuse—a family emergency—and asked another barber to take Jerome's appointment. Since then, he has found himself scanning each client as they walk through the door, watching for signs of threat. A man who glances around the shop too long. Someone who stands too close. The hypervigilance exhausted him.

At home, Kofi began to withdraw. Ama would ask him simple questions—how was work, did he eat lunch—and he would snap at her, convinced that she was criticizing him, judging him for what had happened. In his mind, the robbery became evidence of his failure. He should have locked the door sooner. He should have seen them coming. He should have fought back. He dwelled on these thoughts obsessively, turning them over like stones in his pocket, each rotation a fresh wound. The more he blamed himself, the more he avoided being around people. He stopped going to his church, stopped accepting invitations from friends. He spent his evenings in the back room of the shop, ostensibly organizing supplies, but really just sitting in the dark, trying hard not to think about that night—pushing the images away with a force that left him exhausted.

His work began to suffer. He was slower, less attentive. Two clients complained that he seemed distant, distracted. One asked if everything was all right. The question felt like an accusation. Last week, Ama found him in the garage at midnight, unable to sleep, unable to explain why. She finally insisted he talk to someone. Kofi came to his first appointment terrified that speaking about the robbery would make it real in a way that silence had not. He is most afraid that the images will never stop, that he will never find the words to make sense of what happened, and that the man he was before September will remain forever locked outside the barbershop door.
